cards.title: Create Physical Products with Weight to Enable Shipping
cards.summary: Turning on product weight is required so Shopify treats an item as physical and offers shipping rates.
cards.use_when: Adding a new physical product in Shopify admin and configuring shipping eligibility.
steps: When creating the product, enable the weight field; otherwise Shopify treats the product as digital and will not present shipping options.
Enter the product weight (e.g. 0.25) and change the unit as needed to match your warehouse and carrier conventions.
Optional: add customs/duties-related information for cross-border shipping from the same area.
Save, then verify the weight by checking the product in the Shipping settings or by previewing checkout rates for a destination.
caveats: Applies to physical goods; digital products intentionally skip weight.
Weight units affect calculated carrier rates — keep them consistent across the catalog.

cards.title: Set Up Product Variants for Size and Color
cards.summary: Add variant options so one product listing offers all sizes and colors with per-variant pricing, stock, and images.
cards.use_when: Listing apparel or any product that comes in multiple sizes, colors, or materials.
steps: In the product editor, scroll to Variants and click Add options; add the first option such as Size and list values (Small, Medium, Large), then Done.
Add a second option such as Color; Shopify links variant colors to the product's category meta fields automatically.
Assign an image to each variant so shoppers see the right photo when they select a combination.
Edit price and quantity per variant (e.g. 100 units each) if they differ; confirm quantities are accurate before saving.
Click Save; if you use exotic colors or patterns, plan to set up color swatches later rather than relying on default names.
caveats: Variant options are limited by Shopify's maximum option/combination constraints — verify current limit in the admin.
Multiple images per single variant requires specific (often paid) themes.

cards.title: Build Manual vs Smart Collections
cards.summary: Smart collections auto-populate by rules like tags, vendor, price, or inventory, and the type is locked once created.
cards.use_when: Organizing a catalog into collections that stay current as products are added.
steps: Go to Products > Collections and click Add collection.
Name the collection and optionally add a description and image.
Choose Manual (hand-pick products) or Smart (rule-based); once saved the type cannot be switched, so decide with future catalog growth in mind.
For Smart collections, set a condition such as product tag equals 'leggings' so any tagged product joins automatically.
Alternative rules include product type, category, vendor (e.g. Adidas), weight, or inventory stock (e.g. only items with 10 units left).
Save and confirm the collection's condition displays correctly in the collections list.
caveats: You cannot convert manual to smart or vice versa after creation — plan ahead for large catalogs.
Tag-based collections require consistent tag spelling across products or items will not appear.

cards.title: Tag Products Consistently for Smart Collections
cards.summary: Standardized product tags drive reliable smart collections, and inconsistent spelling silently excludes products.
cards.use_when: Assigning tags to products so collections, filters, and navigation stay organized.
steps: Decide on a small, consistent tag vocabulary (e.g. leggings, bras, accessories, overalls) before tagging.
In each product, add the exact tag text — copy and paste to avoid typos like 'bras' vs 'bra'.
Build smart collections with conditions matching those tags (tag equals leggings, tag equals accessories).
After saving, refresh the collections view; updates can take a few seconds to propagate.
If a product is missing, verify its tag spelling and re-save.
Only tag products with the category they are sold under to keep collections clean.
caveats: Smart collections depend on exact tag matching; small typos break the rule silently.
Tags can be edited later, but bulk changes may need third-party apps when Shopify's bulk editor is limited.

cards.title: Use Bulk Edit for Prices, Quantities, and Tags
cards.summary: Shopify's spreadsheet-style bulk editor updates many products at once but has limits that may require a third-party app.
cards.use_when: Cleaning up prices, stock levels, or tags across a large product catalog.
steps: Go to Products, select products, and click Bulk edit to open the spreadsheet-style view.
Use Columns to choose which fields are visible (e.g. price, inventory, tags).
Fill in missing prices or quantities; drag values down across rows like a spreadsheet.
For inventory, confirm 'track quantity' status per product and set quantities (e.g. 100) where missing.
For tags, add consistent values such as 'accessories' or 'leggings' so future smart collections catch them.
Save and re-verify in the products list and collections.
caveats: Bulk edit has limitations; complex changes may require a dedicated bulk-editing third-party app.
Tag changes propagate to smart collections only after a short delay or refresh.

cards.title: Edit Product Images In-Shopify: Crop, Resize, Remove Background
cards.summary: Shopify's built-in image tools handle cropping, resizing, background removal, and background generation at the product level.
cards.use_when: Fixing inconsistent product photos or making PDP images match your visual standards without external tools.
steps: Open a product, click an image, and use the built-in tools.
Crop to a fixed ratio (e.g. square) when images are inconsistent.
Rotate, flip, or resize to a specific pixel size.
Use background removal to strip the background and apply a solid color like white for consistent PDP backgrounds.
Optionally use the AI background generator with a text prompt (e.g. 'outdoor garden') to place the product in a scene, but expect occasional failures.
Choose Save in place or Save as new; saving as new keeps the original and adds the edited image to the product.
caveats: The built-in AI background generator can fail or produce mediocre results; dedicated tools like Canva may be stronger for complex edits.
AI-generated backgrounds may not match brand aesthetics — review before saving to the live PDP.

cards.title: Generate Product Images with Sidekick AI
cards.summary: Shopify's Sidekick can generate lifestyle product images from a product photo and a prompt, iterating conversationally.
cards.use_when: Creating lifestyle or contextual imagery for product pages or ads when you lack photoshoots.
steps: From the Shopify dashboard, click the Sidekick icon to open the AI assistant.
Upload or paste your product image into the Sidekick conversation.
Write a simple prompt describing the scene you want (e.g. 'show someone drinking this coffee in an office').
If the first result is illogical, refine the prompt (e.g. 'show someone holding the coffee in their hands') and regenerate.
Save the resulting image file from the Sidekick chat and upload it to the product or page.
Verify the current interface, as Sidekick's capabilities and access change with Shopify releases.
caveats: Access to Sidekick and its image generation may vary by store and Shopify plan; the interface has changed in recent editions.
AI images can look unrealistic for some niches — review against brand standards before publishing.

cards.title: Configure Variant Color Swatches with Hex or Pattern Images
cards.summary: Shopify assigns default variant colors from category meta fields; you can override with exact hex codes or pattern images.
cards.use_when: Setting up color swatches for a product where default swatch colors are inaccurate or you sell patterns/textures.
steps: In the product editor, look under the linked category meta field for colors.
Replace default color names by editing entries; add new entries like 'dark blue' or 'dark green' via Add new entry.
Provide an exact hex code (search Google for the color hex if needed) so the swatch matches the real product color.
For patterns, textures, or uncertain colors (e.g. lip butter texture), upload a label image instead of a hex code.
Save and assign variant images for each color.
Note: showing only selected-variant images on the PDP requires theme support — often paid themes, not free ones.
caveats: Default Shopify color extraction is not accurate — always verify or override.
Some themes (usually paid) support variant-specific image display; free themes often do not, and setup differs per theme.

cards.title: Set Up Storefront Filters with the Search and Discovery App
cards.summary: Shopify's free Search and Discovery app controls which filters (price, availability, category meta fields, or custom) appear on collection pages.
cards.use_when: Adding filterable navigation to a collection page so shoppers can narrow a large catalog by attributes.
steps: Install the free Shopify Search and Discovery app.
Open Filters; Shopify starts with availability and price — remove those that don't fit your catalog.
Click Add filter and pick a source: category meta fields, standard fields like vendor/brand, or your own product meta fields.
Save and verify on the storefront that the right filter values exist for products in the collection.
To check which categories a meta field applies to, go to Settings > Custom data > Products > Assigned to categories.
Filter options to consider: brand, color, size, availability, sport type, waist style, length — driven by what shoppers actually search for.
caveats: Filters only appear if the underlying meta field values are populated on products.
The app's UI and available sources change with Shopify updates — verify the current interface.

cards.title: Create Custom Product Filters When Category Meta Fields Fall Short
cards.summary: Custom product meta fields let you add filters beyond Shopify's category defaults and apply them across all products.
cards.use_when: Adding a filter attribute your niche needs that isn't in the default category meta fields.
steps: Go to Settings > Custom data (meta fields and meta objects) > Products, then Add definition.
Name it (e.g. 'trial filter') and choose a type; 'list of values' lets one product appear under multiple values (e.g. gold and white gold).
Set the input type (e.g. single line text) and assign it to categories or leave it open for all products.
Save, then fill the meta field per product (or bulk edit across products).
Return to the Search and Discovery app, Add filter, and choose the new product meta field as the source.
Verify on the collection page after saving.
caveats: If left unassigned to categories, the field appears on all products — which may add confusion for categories where it doesn't apply.
Values must be populated per product or the filter shows empty.

cards.title: Choose Filters from Customer Search Language
cards.summary: Filters should reflect how shoppers search and what competitors in the niche expose, not every attribute you have.
cards.use_when: Deciding which filters to expose on category pages for a new or existing store.
steps: Review your product categories in Shopify to see default meta fields Shopify pre-assigns (e.g. yoga mats get color, material).
Study competitors and large stores in your niche to see which filters they surface.
List questions customers commonly ask and the ways they describe products (e.g. 'cotton leggings', 'ankle length', 'black leggings').
Select only filters that map to real search intent — don't include every available attribute.
For stores with large catalogs, plan filters early so the catalog stays organized as it grows.
caveats: This is the presenter's recommended approach, not a universal rule; small catalogs may need fewer filters.
Over-filtering with rarely used attributes clutters collection pages and can hurt navigation.

cards.title: Filter Shopify Themes by Industry, Catalog Size, and Required Features
cards.summary: Use Shopify theme store filters to narrow hundreds of themes down to a shortlist matching your niche, catalog size, and required sections.
cards.use_when: Shortlisting candidate Shopify themes before committing to a design foundation.
steps: In the theme store, filter by Industry to see demo themes closest to your niche (e.g. Beauty).
Filter by Catalog size: modest catalogs (roughly 11–100 products) differ from large (500+) stores, which need heavier search and navigation.
Filter by Features: e.g. before/after slider for cosmetics, color swatches, combined listing, age verifier for regulated goods.
Prioritize paid themes ($100–$400 one-time) when the source's experience suggests free themes often lack features and polish; the source's opinion, not a universal rule.
Open the demo store, check the PDP layout and section list, and read the reviews.
Inspect the developer: click through to their profile, check how many themes they publish, and search the company on Google to gauge legitimacy.
caveats: Filters may over-narrow results (e.g. only 20 themes for combined listing) — relax filters if the shortlist is too small.
The source's preference for paid themes is a personal opinion; free themes can work for simple stores.

cards.title: Preview Mobile and Desktop Before Buying a Theme
cards.summary: Always check a theme's mobile demo since most traffic is mobile, and shortlist only themes whose mobile experience holds up.
cards.use_when: Evaluating theme candidates before purchase or trial installation.
steps: On the theme's page, click View demo to open the full desktop storefront.
Scroll through home and PDP sections to evaluate layout, social proof placement (UGC video, before/after), and section variety.
Check the mobile preview or open the demo URL on a phone; mobile is where most shoppers land.
Note which sections exist in any demo preset of the same theme — features seen in one preset apply across the theme.
Keep only themes whose mobile layout meets your standard; discard the rest.
caveats: Demo stores may use different presets; confirm the feature you want actually exists in the theme settings.
This is preparatory research, not a substitute for testing the theme with your own catalog.

cards.title: Trial a Theme Before Buying to Preserve Work
cards.summary: Shopify lets you install a full theme trial, customize it, and buy later without losing changes.
cards.use_when: Deciding between finalist themes before committing to a purchase.
steps: Confirm you are signed into the correct Shopify store.
Click Try theme on the theme's store page; Shopify adds a full trial version you can edit but not publish.
Open the theme editor and build out key sections (home, PDP, coming soon page) to test fit.
If satisfied, click Buy; all your changes are preserved and the theme becomes publishable.
Optional: before upgrading, duplicate the theme via the three-dot menu to back it up (or use a backup app).
caveats: Some features — e.g. editing theme code or using product page templates — may require purchase first; verify current limitations.
Trial versions cannot be published to customers.

cards.title: Duplicate Your Theme as a Backup Before Big Changes
cards.summary: Duplicating the theme creates a safe restore point before customizations or updates.
cards.use_when: Before large theme edits, version pushes, or any risky change to a live storefront.
steps: Go to Online Store > Themes.
Click the three dots next to the theme and choose Duplicate.
Rename the duplicate clearly (e.g. 'backup pre-update').
Use third-party theme backup apps if you need scheduled or versioned backups that Shopify's built-in duplication doesn't cover.
Verify the duplicate appears in the theme list before proceeding with the risky change.
caveats: Built-in duplication gives a snapshot, not automated version history; apps provide more robust backups.
Duplicating is not a substitute for testing changes in a trial or unpublished theme first.

cards.title: Set Up a Password-Protected Coming Soon Page
cards.summary: Every Shopify store is password-locked by default and the 'password' theme controls what visitors see pre-launch.
cards.use_when: Preparing to launch a store or keep a site private while building it.
steps: By default the store is protected; visitors see the coming soon (password) page instead of the storefront.
Go to Online Store > Themes > Password theme and start customizing — it works like any other theme page.
To preview what customers see, open your store's domain in an incognito window (avoid the logged-in admin view).
The password required to unlock the store is set under Settings > Preferences (or the account's password page settings) — share it only with intended viewers.
Remove the lock when the store is ready to launch.
caveats: Forgetting the store password or leaving the lock on post-launch blocks all customer traffic.
The exact settings path may shift with Shopify releases — verify in your admin.

cards.title: Reject One-Click AI Whole-Store Theming; Design for Conversion
cards.summary: Shopify's instant AI store generator may shortchange the conversion-focused design work that a curated theme delivers.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to launch with an auto-generated theme or to design the storefront deliberately.
steps: Optional test: run Shopify's AI theme generator (e.g. with a prompt like 'active wear brand') to see the generated layout.
Treat the output as a starting idea, not a final storefront — the source is not a fan of the feature and prefers building step-by-step.
Design for conversion, not only aesthetics: make information legible, products easy to explore, and social proof visible.
Aim to convert visitors into first-time buyers and repeat customers, not just to look polished.
If the theme lacks needed sections, consider a paid theme or theme AI editor tools rather than forcing the auto-generated layout.
caveats: Availability of the AI theme generator varies by store and Shopify plan.
This is the presenter's opinion; some merchants may find the generated themes a useful starting point.

cards.title: Plan Theme Around Site Structure and Future Catalog
cards.summary: Theme choice is a multi-year decision — pick based on the features, sections, and catalog growth you expect, not just today's look.
cards.use_when: Committing to a theme for a store you plan to grow over years.
steps: Before browsing themes, list the features/sections you want (visual effects, product recommendations, comparison tables, ingredient panels, UGC, before/after sliders).
Do competitor research and note the sections and layouts you want to emulate.
Accept that the theme is a one-time, multi-year choice — changing later means redoing setup and settings across the store.
Prefer themes from proven developers when planning to stay on the theme for years, since they maintain updates.
Use the theme store's filters and the demo browser to shortlist and compare candidate themes.
Keep in mind that the Shopify editor's logic applies across themes even if exact settings differ — you are learning the process, not one theme's menu.
caveats: Theme migration later is possible but time-consuming; the presenter treats this as a major commitment.
The theme's AI section-building tools are described as glitchy and inconsistent — don't rely on them as the primary customization method.
